CSS: .chips{position:sticky;top:0;z-index:20;display:flex;gap:8px;overflow-x:auto;scroll-snap-type:x proximity;padding:12px 16px;background:rgba(255,251,244,.92);backdrop-filter:blur(10px);-webkit-backdrop-filter:blur(10px)}.chips::-webkit-scrollbar{display:none}.chip{scroll-snap-align:start;white-space:nowrap;padding:8px 16px;border:2px solid #382900;border-radius:999px;color:#382900;font-weight:700;box-shadow:2px 2px 0 #382900}.chip.active{background:var(--brand);color:#fff}. html{scroll-behavior:smooth}. Section anchors need scroll-margin-top so the sticky bar doesn't cover the heading: section{scroll-margin-top:64px}. Scroll-spy JS: const spy=new IntersectionObserver((es)=>{es.forEach(e=>{if(e.isIntersecting){document.querySelectorAll('.chip').forEach(c=>c.classList.toggle('active',c.hash==='#'+e.target.id));document.querySelector('.chip.active')?.scrollIntoView({inline:'center',block:'nearest'})}})},{rootMargin:'-45% 0px -50% 0px'});document.querySelectorAll('section[id]').forEach(s=>spy.observe(s)). The rootMargin band picks the section crossing mid-screen as active; the active chip auto-centers itself in the strip. For AR set dir=rtl on the page root and the flex + scroll mirror automatically; use box-shadow offset 2px 2px (the confident ink offset, Godzilla law #2) not a blurred shadow.

patterns.name: Founding-Myth Hero (per-cafe mini-world)
patterns.what: The hero isn't 'Logo + tagline + View Menu'. It's a 2-3 line micro-story that names a place, a year, and a feeling unique to THIS cafe — e.g. AR: 'في زاوية من الرياض، فنجان يبدأ الحكاية' / EN: 'In a quiet corner of Riyadh, a cup begins the story.' The animated brand mark assembles on load, then the name, then the story line fades up beneath it. This is Dishoom's proven 'each location is a dedicated mini-world with its own founding myth' idea, compressed to one phone screen.
patterns.why_it_wins: Dishoom's whole reputation rests on 'design as storytelling' — every venue gets an imagined main character and raison d'etre, and reviewers literally say 'you scroll and feel culture.' A Riyadh owner comparing menus in 3 seconds in a coffee queue feels SEEN when the first screen is about their shop's soul, not a generic 'Welcome to our cafe.' It instantly separates you from template/AI menus that all open identically.
patterns.how_to_apply:
Full-viewport hero:

Keep myth line INK-dark (brand-ink ~#382900), max ~9 words; store per cafe as {mythAr, mythEn, year, place}. Add a soft downward chevron with @keyframes bob to invite the scroll. Respect prefers-reduced-motion by wrapping animations in @media (prefers-reduced-motion:no-preference).

patterns.name: One-Line-Per-Screen Scroll Chapters
patterns.what: Between the hero and the menu, 2-4 short 'chapter' panels each fill one screen with a SINGLE sentence that reveals word-by-word as you scroll (grey -> ink). e.g. Screen: 'We roast for the morning people.' Then: 'Every cup here is measured, not guessed.' Then the menu 'chapter' opens. Built with native CSS scroll-driven animations (animation-timeline: view()).
patterns.why_it_wins: Scrollytelling — 'each scroll position revealing content with intentional pacing' — is exactly what Awwwards/NRK sites win with, and CSS animation-timeline now does it off-main-thread so it stays buttery on a mid-range Android. One confident line per screen reads like a luxury brand film, the opposite of a dense AI wall-of-text menu. It builds anticipation so the prices land after the emotion.
patterns.how_to_apply:
Per chapter:

We roast for the morning people.

with .chapter{min-height:100svh;display:grid;place-items:center}. Word reveal: wrap words in spans, animate on their own view timeline: .line span{opacity:.15;animation:ink linear both;animation-timeline:view();animation-range:cover 20% cover 55%} @keyframes ink{to{opacity:1}}. For per-word stagger, give each span animation-range offsets or use a tiny JS IntersectionObserver fallback that adds .lit sequentially for browsers without scroll timelines (Safari<26). Keep ink color the brand-ink; the un-lit state is the same hue at low opacity, never a different grey, so it never looks broken. Arabic version: same markup with dir=rtl — word order handled by the browser, no letter-spacing (breaks Arabic joins).

patterns.name: Gift / Invitation First-Contact (landing variant)
patterns.what: The gift/landing variant reframes the page as an invitation addressed TO the owner or guest, not an ad. Opens with an envelope/seal motif and a line like AR: 'دعوة خاصة لـ [اسم الكافيه]' / EN: 'A private invitation for [Cafe Name].' A wax-seal or ribbon 'opens' on tap/scroll to reveal the menu beneath. Personalized token ([Cafe Name]) is injected per link.
patterns.why_it_wins: Paperless Post built a business on this exact insight: 'combining personalization with a friendly tone makes guests feel individually valued rather than another number.' For Menu Sadah's sales weapon (the gift links), an owner opening a link that literally says 'invitation for [their cafe]' with a seal that breaks open is an emotional gut-punch no cold DM achieves — it's the 4Us (Unique, Ultra-Specific) made visual. This is the conversion machine, not decoration.
patterns.how_to_apply: Read the name from URL: const cafe=new URLSearchParams(location.search).get('for')||'your cafe'; inject into <h1>. Seal: an SVG circle 'stamp' over the fold; on click OR when it scrolls into view, add .opened -> CSS animates two flap divs rotating away (transform:rotateX(-160deg);transform-origin:top) and the seal scales+fades, revealing content with a staggered rise. Use position:sticky on the seal so it feels like it lifts off the page. Keep the whole thing skippable (seal is decorative; content is in normal flow underneath). Personalize sparingly and truthfully (name only — never invent details, per evidence rule). Bilingual: mirror the ribbon/flap direction under dir=rtl using logical transforms.

patterns.name: Founder-Voice Signature Note
patterns.what: One short handwritten-style note in first person, signed, placed between the menu and the footer (or as chapter 2). ~2 sentences: why this cafe exists, in the owner's voice. AR + EN. Rendered in a warm hand/serif face on a subtle 'paper' card with tape corners and a real-looking signature, plus a tiny animated pen-stroke underline.
patterns.why_it_wins: 2025 restaurant-design consensus: 'team photos, short narratives and founder story convey authenticity and create a personal connection'; Dishoom's designers say plainly 'good design can tell a story... convey even a little of this poetry.' A first-person line makes a cafe feel human and owner-run, which is precisely the emotional lever that makes a Riyadh owner trust YOU to represent their brand. It's cheap to produce and impossible for a generic template to fake convincingly.
patterns.how_to_apply: <figure class="note"> card with border:2px solid ink; box-shadow:4px 4px 0 ink (hard offset, no blur — the confident ink-craft look); slight transform:rotate(-1.2deg). Body in a hand/serif face (self-hosted, never auto-fallback). 'Tape' = two ::before/::after pseudo-elements, semi-opaque tan rectangles rotated at the top corners. Signature: inline SVG <path> drawn with stroke-dasharray/dashoffset animated once on view (@keyframes sign{to{stroke-dashoffset:0}}). Keep the note text INK-dark for legibility. Provide lang/dir pairs so the Arabic note uses an Arabic hand/naskh face and reads RTL. Content must be the REAL owner's words or omitted — no invented quotes.

patterns.name: Bilingual Story Medallion + True RTL Mirroring
patterns.what: A round brand medallion carrying the cafe's initial that FLIPS with the language toggle — Arabic initial in AR mode, Latin initial in EN mode — and the entire narrative (hero myth, chapters, note) swaps direction, not just text. The toggle is a single pill; switching re-flows dir=rtl/ltr, mirrors chevrons/arrows, and swaps the medallion glyph with a quick coin-flip animation.
patterns.why_it_wins: Every source on Saudi design says the same: 'auto-fallback to Latin fonts in Arabic is the signal of a cheap site' and real RTL 'mirrors icons that need mirroring, tests every direction.' Getting this genuinely right (Arabic 10-15% larger, line-height >=1.8, no letter-spacing, proper mirroring) is the difference between 'made for us' and 'translated by a foreigner' — the exact thing a Riyadh owner judges you on. The flipping medallion turns a legal/UX requirement into a delightful brand moment.
patterns.how_to_apply: Toggle sets document.documentElement.dir and .lang; CSS uses logical properties throughout (margin-inline, padding-inline, inset-inline, text-align:start) so layout mirrors for free — never left/right. Type: html[lang=ar]{font-size:112%;line-height:1.85} and NEVER letter-spacing on Arabic. Self-host an Arabic display+text face (e.g. a Cairo/Tajawal/IBM Plex Sans Arabic-class pairing) AND its Latin counterpart; declare unicode-range so each script uses its own font. Medallion: two stacked glyph spans (AR/EN); on toggle add .flip -> transform:rotateY(180deg) on the coin, swap visible glyph at 50% via animationend. Mirror chevrons with [dir=rtl] .chev{transform:scaleX(-1)}. Prices/numerals: keep Western Arabic numerals but set them dir=ltr inside the row so 12.00 never reverses.

patterns.name: Tap-to-Reveal Menu Rows (dish micro-stories)
patterns.what: Menu items stay clean — name + price on one line — but each row is tappable to expand a one-line story or origin/ingredient note beneath it (accordion), with an optional photo sliding in. Category sections are framed as 'chapters' with a titled divider and sticky bilingual category chips that highlight the active section as you scroll.
patterns.why_it_wins: 2025 trend reports call out that 'static menus feel boring — interactive menus where tapping reveals ingredients and subtle animations bring the dish to life' are what premium/late-night brands ship. It keeps the price list scannable (what the owner needs) while rewarding curiosity with story (what makes it feel crafted). The sticky-chip active-section highlight is the small interaction that makes a single scrolling page feel like a real app, not a PDF.
patterns.how_to_apply: Row: <button class="item" aria-expanded="false"> with <span class=name> <span class=price> on a flex row (justify-content:space-between; the price wrapped in dir=ltr). Detail: a sibling <div class=detail> with max-height:0;overflow:hidden;transition:max-height .35s ease; JS toggles aria-expanded and sets .open (max-height to scrollHeight). Photo lazy-loads on first open (loading=lazy) so the page stays fast on cellular. Sticky chips: <nav class=chips style="position:sticky;top:0"> horizontal-scroll row; an IntersectionObserver on each <section> toggles the matching chip's .active class (thick ink underline). Give the active chip scroll-margin and call chip.scrollIntoView({inline:'center'}) so it recenters. Chapter divider: category title with a hard 3px offset-shadow rule and a tiny doodle. All fully keyboard-accessible (real <button>s), and closed state degrades to a plain readable menu if JS fails.

patterns.name: Scroll-driven brew-story hero (native CSS, zero JS)
patterns.what: A full-viewport hero that is position:sticky and stays pinned while ~120vh of scroll plays a mini story on it: the animated brand mark assembles, steam rises off a cup, the cafe name in Arabic + English fades/scales in, then the whole hero shrinks and hands off to the first category. Driven entirely by the 2025 CSS Scroll-driven Animations API (animation-timeline: view()/scroll()) — no GSAP, no ScrollTrigger, no JS. Runs on the compositor thread so it stays 60fps on a cheap phone.
patterns.why_it_wins: This is the single biggest 'this isn't a template' signal in 2025 — Apple/Awwwards-tier scroll choreography that used to need heavy JS now ships in pure CSS and Safari 26 + Firefox both support it. A pinned, self-playing hero reads as a bespoke agency build, not a QR-code generator. It also fights the generic-AI look because the motion is tied to THIS cafe's mark and drink, and it degrades to a normal static hero on old browsers with zero breakage.

patterns.name: Scroll-spy sticky category chips (RTL-aware, IntersectionObserver)
patterns.what: The horizontal category chip row (قهوة | حلا | Cold) sticks under the top on scroll, and the chip for the section you're currently reading auto-highlights and auto-scrolls itself into view inside the strip. Tapping a chip smooth-scrolls to that section. Built with one IntersectionObserver watching the <section>s (not a scroll listener) + scrollIntoView.
patterns.why_it_wins: This is the navigational spine that makes a long single-page menu feel like an app instead of a scroll-forever PDF. The live active-chip is the detail owners notice — it says 'someone engineered this.' It's also the highest-utility premium moment: a customer scanning a QR at a table finds 'cold drinks' in one tap. Cheap to build, huge perceived-quality return.
patterns.how_to_apply:
HTML:
قهوة…
and each section

CSS: .chips{position:sticky;top:0;z-index:20;display:flex;gap:.5rem;overflow-x:auto;scroll-snap-type:x proximity;-webkit-overflow-scrolling:touch}.chip{scroll-snap-align:center;border:2px solid var(--ink);box-shadow:3px 3px 0 var(--ink);border-radius:999px;padding:.4rem .9rem;white-space:nowrap}.chip.active{background:var(--ink);color:var(--cream)}. Also set html{scroll-behavior:smooth;scroll-padding-top:64px} so anchor jumps clear the sticky bar. JS: const obs=new IntersectionObserver(es=>es.forEach(e=>{if(e.isIntersecting){const id=e.target.id;document.querySelectorAll('.chip').forEach(c=>c.classList.toggle('active',c.hash==='#'+id));document.querySelector('.chip.active')?.scrollIntoView({inline:'center',block:'nearest',behavior:'smooth'})}}),{rootMargin:'-45% 0px -50% 0px'}); document.querySelectorAll('section[id]').forEach(s=>obs.observe(s)); RTL: because .chips is flex, dir="rtl" flips chip order automatically and scrollIntoView inline:'center' still works — no extra code.

patterns.name: Gyroscope tilt on the signature-item card
patterns.what: ONE hero card (the cafe's signature drink / most-profitable item) reacts in 3D to how the customer holds the phone: tilting the device rotates the card on X/Y with a soft glare sweep, so the photo and the ink border feel physically raised off the page. Uses DeviceOrientationEvent (beta/gamma) on mobile, falls back to pointermove on desktop. Not a library — ~20 lines of vanilla JS, capped tilt angles so it never looks gimmicky.
patterns.why_it_wins: A single living element among calm static rows is a classic 'signature moment' — it draws the eye exactly to the item you want to sell, and the parallax-on-motion effect is impossible to fake with a paper menu or a Canva template. It reads as expensive precisely because it's restrained (one card, small angles). This is the kind of detail a Riyadh cafe owner shows off to friends.
patterns.how_to_apply:
HTML:
…photo, name, price…
. CSS: .tilt{perspective:800px}.tilt-inner{transition:transform .1s ease-out;transform-style:preserve-3d;border:2px solid var(--ink);box-shadow:6px 6px 0 var(--ink)}.glare{position:absolute;inset:0;background:linear-gradient(105deg,transparent 40%,rgba(255,255,255,.35),transparent 60%);opacity:0;pointer-events:none}. JS core: const el=document.querySelector('#signature .tilt-inner'); const set=(rx,ry)=>{el.style.transform=`rotateX(${rx}deg) rotateY(${ry}deg)`;el.querySelector('.glare').style.opacity=Math.min(Math.abs(rx)+Math.abs(ry),8)/16}. Desktop: card.addEventListener('pointermove',e=>{const r=card.getBoundingClientRect();set((.5-(e.clientY-r.top)/r.height)*8,((e.clientX-r.left)/r.width-.5)*8)}). Mobile: iOS needs a tap to grant permission — on first touch call DeviceOrientationEvent.requestPermission?.().then(...) then window.addEventListener('deviceorientation',e=>set(Math.max(-6,Math.min(6,(e.beta-45)/6)), Math.max(-6,Math.min(6,e.gamma/6)))). Clamp to ±6–8deg. Respect prefers-reduced-motion by skipping the listeners entirely.

patterns.name: Auto day/night menu with bilingual greeting
patterns.what: The menu skins itself to the local hour: warm cream + light ink in the morning, deep espresso-dark with glowing accents at night, plus a matching bilingual greeting in the hero (صباح الخير / Good morning vs مساء الخير / Good evening) and optionally a 'now serving' nudge (breakfast vs late-night). A small sun/moon toggle lets the customer override; choice is remembered in localStorage. Uses a data-theme attribute + CSS custom properties (and light-dark() where supported).
patterns.why_it_wins: A cafe lives on a daily rhythm, and a menu that KNOWS whether it's morning or night feels alive and personal instead of a static file — it's a genuine emotional hook a paper menu can never do. The time-aware Arabic greeting is a delightful, unmistakably-local touch for Riyadh customers. It's also practically free and makes the same page look like two designed products.
patterns.how_to_apply: CSS variables per theme: :root{--cream:#f5ede0;--ink:#382900;--accent:#b06a2c;color-scheme:light} :root[data-theme=night]{--cream:#1b1410;--ink:#f3e9d8;--accent:#e0a24a;color-scheme:dark} then style everything with var(--ink)/var(--cream) and add transition:background .6s,color .6s on body. JS on load: const h=new Date().getHours(); const auto=(h>=18||h<6)?'night':'day'; const saved=localStorage.theme; document.documentElement.dataset.theme = saved || auto; Greeting: document.querySelector('#greet').innerHTML = (auto==='night') ? 'مساء الخيرGood evening' : 'صباح الخيرGood morning'. Toggle button: btn.onclick=()=>{const t=document.documentElement.dataset.theme==='night'?'day':'night';document.documentElement.dataset.theme=t;localStorage.theme=t}. Keep the ink/cream contrast strong in BOTH themes so text never washes out (the Godzilla ink-legibility law applies to night mode too — test the accent isn't used for long text).

patterns.name: Liquid-fill / steam signature moment tied to the hero drink
patterns.what: A single crafted interactive flourish on the cafe's flagship drink: as the signature section scrolls into view, an SVG cup FILLS with coffee (a clip-path/height driven by the scroll position), steam curls up on a loop, and the price 'stamps' in when the cup is full. Pure CSS steam (blurred rising pseudo-elements) + a scroll-driven fill via animation-timeline: view() (or an IntersectionObserver setting a --fill custom property as fallback).
patterns.why_it_wins: It turns the act of scrolling to your best product into a tiny reward — the drink literally gets made as you arrive. This is the 'interactive signature moment' that gets screenshotted and shared, which is free marketing for the cafe. Because it's scoped to ONE drink it stays classy instead of noisy, and it's derived from the cafe's own product so it can never look like a stock template.

patterns.name: Brand-mark easter egg → off-menu secret drink
patterns.what: Tapping the animated brand mark 5 times fast (or the desktop Konami code) unlocks a hidden 'off-menu / سري' card — a real secret drink the owner picks — with a burst of coffee-bean confetti and a soft haptic buzz. State can persist in localStorage so returning regulars keep their unlocked secret. Entirely vanilla JS: a tap counter with a timeout, plus a keydown sequence matcher.
patterns.why_it_wins: Easter eggs are the purest 'a human built this, with love' signal — exactly the thing that makes a menu feel crafted rather than AI-spat. For a cafe it's also a genuine loyalty/marketing mechanic: a secret regulars-only drink is a story customers tell each other, driving repeat visits. It costs nothing, sits invisibly until discovered, and can never read as generic.
patterns.how_to_apply: Tap counter: let taps=0,timer; mark.addEventListener('pointerup',()=>{taps++;clearTimeout(timer);timer=setTimeout(()=>taps=0,600);if(taps>=5){unlock()}}). Konami (desktop): const code=['ArrowUp','ArrowUp','ArrowDown','ArrowDown','ArrowLeft','ArrowRight','ArrowLeft','ArrowRight','b','a'];let i=0;onkeydown=e=>{i=(e.key===code[i])?i+1:0;if(i===code.length)unlock()}. unlock(): document.querySelector('#secret').hidden=false; document.querySelector('#secret').scrollIntoView({behavior:'smooth'}); navigator.vibrate?.(30); localStorage.secret='1'; then spawn ~20 absolutely-positioned bean spans with a fall keyframe (transform:translateY(110vh) rotate) and remove them on animationend. On load: if(localStorage.secret)document.querySelector('#secret').hidden=false. Keep the secret card fully bilingual (سري / Secret) and in-brand (same ink border + accent). No hint in the UI — discovery is the point; owner can tell regulars where to tap.

patterns.name: Staggered ink-craft reveal-on-scroll for item rows
patterns.what: Instead of a dead static list, each item row (name … price) rises + fades in with a small stagger as its category scrolls into view, using per-element view() timelines so rows animate on THEIR own entrance (not all at once). The motion is short and confident — a 12px lift + fade, matched to the hand-drawn ink aesthetic — never bouncy or slow. Native CSS scroll-driven animation, with an IntersectionObserver fallback and full reduced-motion respect.
patterns.why_it_wins: It's the cheapest way to make a long menu feel choreographed and alive rather than a wall of text, and because each row reveals as you reach it, the page feels responsive to the reader. Done subtly it reads premium (editorial, considered); done natively it costs almost nothing in performance. It's the connective tissue that makes all the bigger moments (hero, tilt, fill) feel part of one crafted system.
